paragraphs: The paper studies social decisions through the hypothesis that people maintain uncertain beliefs about other people's intentions and willingness to cooperate. It represents this reasoning with a partially observable Markov decision process, or POMDP. In this framework, decisions depend on probabilistic beliefs about information that cannot be directly observed and on the rewards expected from different actions.

The authors apply the model to the volunteer's dilemma in a version of the Public Goods Game. They report that two interpretable parameters are sufficient to model subjects' decisions across the trials. This connects observed choices to a compact account of how uncertainty about others and anticipated rewards can influence social behavior.

The study also relates the model to brain activity measured with fMRI. Model predictions of each subject's expected reward correlated with activity in areas associated with reward expectation during social interactions. Together, the behavioral and neural findings support the proposed probabilistic account; they suggest, rather than establish universally, that social decisions can reflect expected reward maximization.
neurips-2016-a-probabilistic-model-of-so.tldr: A probabilistic reward-maximization model accounts for choices in a social game and links predicted rewards to measured brain activity.

paragraphs: The paper examines how averaging can accelerate constrained convex optimization. Its starting point is a continuous-time description with two coupled quantities: a dual variable that accumulates gradients, and a primal variable formed by averaging the mirrored dual trajectory. The gradient accumulation rate and the averaging weights jointly determine how this process evolves.

Using a Lyapunov function, a quantity used to track progress, the authors derive sufficient conditions on these rates and weights for a desired convergence rate. One example shows that averaging can accelerate replicator dynamics, a form of mirror descent on the simplex. This makes the choice of averaging rule an explicit part of the acceleration mechanism.

The authors then propose choosing weights adaptively to make the Lyapunov function decrease faster. They establish continuous-time guarantees and show that the discrete-time version preserves the quadratic convergence rate of accelerated first-order methods. Numerical comparisons indicate performance at least as good as adaptive restarting in the reported experiments, with substantial improvements in some cases.
neurips-2016-adaptive-averaging-in-accel.tldr: Adaptive averaging can accelerate convex optimization while preserving the convergence rate of accelerated first-order methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies a restricted form of nonconvex optimization: the objective may be irregular, but its value stays within a fixed error tolerance of some convex function at every point. This uniform closeness defines the approximately convex class under consideration. The goal is to find a point whose objective value is within a requested accuracy of the true minimum.

Two different errors therefore matter. One measures how far the objective can deviate from convexity; the other measures the optimization accuracy being requested. The central question is how these quantities interact. Being close to a convex function gives useful structure, but the allowable deviations can still obstruct accurate optimization.

The authors substantially strengthen information-theoretic lower bounds describing this tradeoff. They also provide an algorithm that matches those bounds for a large class of convex bodies. Matching upper and lower bounds identifies what can be achieved within that setting and what the available information cannot support, rather than extending guarantees to arbitrary nonconvex objectives.
neurips-2016-algorithms-and-matching-low.tldr: The paper sharpens limits on approximately convex optimization and gives an algorithm matching them for a broad class of convex domains.

paragraphs: The paper addresses learning when labels provide incomplete or unreliable supervision. Its scope includes semi-supervised learning, learning from label proportions, multi-instance learning, and learning with noisy labels. These settings differ in what is known about the desired outputs, motivating a shared way to express the information available for training.

The proposed beta-risk generalizes standard empirical risk built from surrogate margin-based losses. Its key feature is the ability to represent label reliability within the training objective. This makes the treatment of uncertain supervision part of the risk formulation itself and provides a basis for deriving different learning algorithms within one framework.

The authors develop this idea specifically for support vector machines, introducing a soft-margin beta-SVM. They report that this algorithm performs better than the state of the art in the work presented. The contribution therefore combines a general formulation for weak supervision with a concrete classifier, connecting a flexible account of label reliability to an operational learning method.
neurips-2016-beta-risk-a-new-surrogate-r.tldr: Beta-risk incorporates label reliability into a general learning objective and yields a soft-margin SVM for weak supervision.

paragraphs: The paper considers combining probabilistic models trained on separate local data repositories into one statistical model. This arises in distributed and privacy-preserving learning. Simply averaging model parameters can produce degenerate results for nonconvex models, and may not even be applicable when the local models have different numbers of parameters.

An alternative is to generate bootstrap samples from each local model and train a joint model on the pooled synthetic observations. This moves aggregation from parameter space to generated data, making it a practical option when parameter averaging is unsuitable. However, the sampling step introduces additional randomness that can substantially degrade the resulting statistical estimates.

The authors propose two variance-reduction methods to correct this bootstrap noise. One is a weighted M-estimator, which they describe as both statistically efficient and practically effective. Theoretical and empirical analyses support the methods. The contribution addresses the extra uncertainty introduced by model aggregation itself, improving the bootstrap route to combining locally trained models.
neurips-2016-bootstrap-model-aggregation.tldr: Two variance-reduction methods improve bootstrap aggregation of distributed probabilistic models by correcting noise from generated samples.

paragraphs: Compressive sensing MRI aims to reconstruct an image from fewer measurements in k-space, reducing the data acquisition needed for a scan. This paper proposes ADMM-Net to improve reconstruction accuracy and computational speed. The architecture starts from the iterative steps of ADMM, an optimization algorithm used to solve a compressive sensing reconstruction model.

The authors turn those steps into a data-flow graph whose parameters can be learned jointly. Image transforms and shrinkage functions are among the components trained end to end using L-BFGS. The resulting network therefore retains a structure derived from an existing reconstruction procedure while adapting its parameters to the reconstruction task through training data.

At test time, ADMM-Net has computational overhead similar to ADMM, but uses its learned parameters. Experiments at different k-space sampling ratios show significant improvements over the baseline ADMM algorithm, alongside high reconstruction accuracy and fast computation. The findings support learning the components of an optimization-derived architecture as a useful approach to MRI reconstruction.
neurips-2016-deep-admm-net-for-compressi.tldr: ADMM-Net turns an MRI reconstruction algorithm into a trainable network that improves reconstruction while retaining similar computational overhead.

paragraphs: The paper estimates an unknown continuous probability density from independent, identically distributed observations. It uses a nonparametric representation: the domain is divided into regions, and the estimated density is constant inside each region. This produces a piecewise constant approximation without committing to a particular parametric family for the underlying distribution.

The regions form a binary partition, built through a sequential splitting process. The distinctive ingredient is discrepancy, a concept drawn from quasi-Monte Carlo analysis, which controls how the partition develops. Consequently, the construction of the regions is a central part of learning the density, rather than merely a preliminary choice of representation.

The authors describe the resulting algorithm as simple and efficient and establish a convergence rate. They also provide empirical evidence of its efficiency for density estimation. Beyond estimating probabilities, they show that the method can provide good initializations for k-means. This connects the learned partitioned density to a second practical task: choosing useful starting points for clustering.
neurips-2016-density-estimation-via-disc.tldr: A discrepancy-guided binary partition produces an efficient density estimator with a convergence guarantee and applications to k-means initialization.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to extract dynamical patterns from finite sequences generated by a nonlinear system without explicitly knowing its governing equations. It builds on the Koopman operator, which describes the evolution of observable quantities through an infinite-dimensional linear operator. Spectral analysis of this operator provides a modal description of the underlying dynamics.

The authors place this analysis in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Their algorithm constructs orthogonal bases for a Krylov matrix in that space, then projects the Koopman operator onto the subspace those bases span. An eigendecomposition of the projected operator yields a finite collection of modes describing the observed dynamics.

This finite representation also serves as a feature extraction procedure. Rather than using the decomposition only to study the system, the authors consider using its extracted features in machine learning applications. Illustrations with synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the approach. The contribution connects operator-based analysis of nonlinear dynamics with a computable representation derived from finite observations.
neurips-2016-dynamic-mode-decomposition-.tldr: A kernel-based Koopman analysis extracts finitely many dynamical modes from observed sequences for analysis and machine learning.

paragraphs: The paper examines a mismatch between a common symmetry assumption in network models and the sparsity of many real networks. Under traditional vertex exchangeability, relabeling vertices does not change the graph distribution. The abstract invokes the Aldous-Hoover result that such graphs are dense or empty with probability one, creating a difficulty for modeling sparse structures.

The authors instead introduce edge exchangeability: the distribution of a graph sequence is unchanged when the order of its edges changes. They demonstrate that models with this symmetry can exhibit sparsity. The result shows that exchangeability itself need not rule out sparse graphs; the objects over which symmetry is imposed matter.

Their generative framework is stationary across steps of the graph sequence. As the dataset grows, the graph expands by instantiating additional latent atoms from a single random measure, rather than adding atoms to that measure. This provides a specific mechanism for graph growth while maintaining the framework's underlying probabilistic structure across successive observations.
neurips-2016-edge-exchangeable-graphs-an.tldr: Replacing vertex exchangeability with edge exchangeability allows random graph models that can be sparse and stationary across graph-sequence steps.

paragraphs: The paper addresses the difficulty of guaranteeing globally optimal neural-network training. Neural-network objectives are highly nonconvex, and stochastic gradient methods generally require parameter tuning without guaranteeing a global optimum. The authors focus on a particular class of feedforward networks, identified in the title as generalized polynomial neural networks.

For this class, they present a method with a global-optimality guarantee and a linear convergence rate under assumptions on the data that they characterize as relatively weak. The title identifies nonlinear spectral methods as the approach. The guarantee is tied to the specified network class and data assumptions, making those conditions central to the result's meaning.

Although the method can in principle extend to deep networks, the paper studies networks with one or two hidden layers for simplicity. Experiments on several real-world datasets show that these models already achieve good performance. The work thus brings together a conditional optimization guarantee and evidence that the covered models have useful representational capacity in practice.
neurips-2016-globally-optimal-training-o.tldr: Under stated data assumptions, a particular class of polynomial neural networks admits globally optimal training with linear convergence.

paragraphs: The paper studies online combinatorial optimization when some actions become unavailable in each round. This is called the sleeping setting. The starting point is a collection of problems that have efficient no-regret algorithms when actions remain available. The authors ask what happens to computational tractability when availability changes during the sequence of decisions.

They show that the sleeping versions are at least as hard as PAC learning disjunctive normal form expressions, a longstanding open learning problem. This is a relative hardness result: an efficient solution to the sleeping problems would also address that difficult learning task. It therefore identifies a substantial computational barrier without proving an unconditional impossibility.

The result covers online shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, k-subsets, k-truncated permutations, minimum cuts, and bipartite matching. For shortest paths, it resolves a previously posed open question. Across these different structures, the shared lesson is that varying action availability can fundamentally change the difficulty of online learning, even when the corresponding always-available problem has efficient no-regret methods.
neurips-2016-hardness-of-online-sleeping.tldr: Several online optimization problems become at least as hard as PAC learning DNF expressions when actions can become unavailable.

paragraphs: Recognition networks provide approximate posterior distributions for directed generative models, making variational inference and learning possible for flexible model families. However, their capacity is limited. An inadequate posterior approximation can restrict what the generative model learns and increase the variability of Monte Carlo estimates used during training.

The paper introduces an iterative procedure that refines the posterior approximation produced by a recognition network. Instead of treating the network's initial proposal as the final inference result, the procedure improves that proposal through additional refinement. Training then uses the refined posterior, directly connecting better approximate inference to the learning process.

The authors report that training with refinement is competitive with state-of-the-art methods. They also find an increase in effective sample size, indicating that the samples provide more useful information for estimation and implying lower variance in gradient estimates. These findings support refinement as a way to address the recognition network's inference bottleneck while improving the statistical quality of the training signal.
neurips-2016-iterative-refinement-of-the.tldr: Iteratively refining a recognition network's posterior approximation yields competitive training results and lower-variance gradient estimates.

paragraphs: The paper extends convolutional neural networks to geometric data whose structure is non-Euclidean. Ordinary convolutions are not directly suited to such domains, which limits their use in graphics and geometry processing. The proposed Anisotropic Convolutional Neural Network, or ACNN, changes the convolution operation to accommodate this kind of data.

ACNN replaces classical convolutions with projections onto oriented anisotropic diffusion kernels. These kernels incorporate direction-dependent structure into the operation. The authors apply the architecture to learning dense correspondences between deformable shapes: the task of identifying matching locations across shapes whose appearance or configuration can change. The correspondences are intrinsic, relating to the shapes' own geometry.

The authors evaluate ACNN in challenging correspondence settings and report state-of-the-art results on some difficult recent benchmarks. The contribution is both architectural and application-focused: it provides a generalization of convolution to non-Euclidean domains and demonstrates its usefulness for a central geometry-processing task. The reported results support the value of orientation-sensitive geometric operations for learning shape correspondence.
neurips-2016-learning-shape-corresponden.tldr: ACNN uses oriented anisotropic diffusion kernels to learn dense correspondences between deformable shapes, achieving strong benchmark results.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to train Supervised PageRank models by minimizing a nonconvex loss. These ranking models can incorporate features of both nodes and edges, allowing the learned ranking to reflect information beyond the graph's connections alone. The optimization problem is therefore a central part of fitting the ranking model to a task.

The authors propose two approaches: a gradient-based method and a randomized gradient-free method. Both are developed around an inexact oracle, meaning that the optimization framework accommodates approximate information supplied to the algorithm. This common perspective lets the paper analyze methods that use different kinds of information to guide their updates.

The main theoretical contribution is a convergence-rate guarantee for each method, which the authors contrast with the existing state-of-the-art gradient-based approach. They also compare the proposed methods with the state of the art on a ranking task. The abstract establishes the presence of that empirical comparison, while the stated advance is the availability of convergence guarantees for both optimization routes.
neurips-2016-learning-supervised-pageran.tldr: Two inexact-oracle optimization methods provide convergence-rate guarantees for training nonconvex Supervised PageRank models.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn strategic interactions from observed data using tree-structured potential games. In this representation, an underlying potential function summarizes the game, and its local maxima correspond to equilibria. Learning therefore involves recovering a structure in which observed joint behavior can be understood through locally stable outcomes.

The authors formulate this task as a maximum-margin learning problem. They show that the problem is NP-hard even when the strategic interaction structure is a tree. The tree restriction therefore does not by itself make the learning problem computationally easy, despite giving the interactions a relatively simple organization.

To estimate the game, the authors develop a variant of dual decomposition. Experiments with synthetic data and real decision and voting data demonstrate meaningful recovery using this game-theoretic perspective. The significance lies in learning which configurations form local maxima of a potential function: that focus provides a way to interpret data as outcomes of strategic interaction while confronting the difficulty of the associated estimation problem.
neurips-2016-learning-tree-structured-po.tldr: Learning tree-structured potential games is NP-hard, but a dual-decomposition approach demonstrates meaningful recovery from decision and voting data.

paragraphs: Machine learning uses many optimization methods tailored to particular regression or classification objectives. This paper asks how a method designed for one setting can be reused in others. Its focus is on differences in smoothness and strong convexity, two properties that shape the optimization problems encountered across learning applications.

The authors develop black-box reductions that take an existing method and apply it across this range of objective properties. Such reductions make algorithm design more reusable: a solver developed for one setting becomes a component in solving other settings. The paper claims optimal reductions that are also more practical than existing alternatives.

The authors show that these reductions yield new, faster training running times for linear classifiers using several families of loss functions. Experiments also demonstrate practical success. The contribution thus links a general technique for transferring optimization methods to concrete improvements in classifier training, reducing the need to design a separate optimization approach for every combination of objective properties.
neurips-2016-optimal-black-box-reduction.tldr: Optimal black-box reductions reuse optimization methods across objective classes and yield faster training algorithms for linear classifiers.

paragraphs: Teacher forcing trains a recurrent network with observed sequence values as inputs, while generating a sequence requires feeding back the network's own predictions. These two modes can produce different internal dynamics. Professor Forcing addresses this mismatch by encouraging the recurrent network to behave similarly during training and during generation over multiple steps.

The method uses adversarial domain adaptation to align those dynamics. The authors apply it to language modeling, raw-waveform vocal synthesis, handwriting generation, and image generation. Its target is the network's evolving behavior across a sequence, making the relationship between training and extended sampling an explicit part of the learning procedure.

Empirically, Professor Forcing acts as a regularizer and improves test likelihood on character-level Penn Treebank and sequential MNIST. Generated samples also improve qualitatively, especially for longer sequences, with human evaluations supporting the quality findings. Visualizations show more similar dynamics between training and sampling. These observations support the proposed alignment mechanism, while the paper also discusses tradeoffs with Scheduled Sampling.
neurips-2016-professor-forcing-a-new-alg.tldr: Professor Forcing aligns recurrent-network dynamics during training and generation, empirically improving likelihood and sample quality.

paragraphs: Random projections reduce the dimensionality of data for learning and search. This paper studies estimating cosine similarity after each projected value has also been quantized to a fixed number of bits. Quantization introduces a nonlinear transformation, so similarity estimation must account for more than the dimensionality reduction alone.

The authors argue for maximum likelihood estimation as a principled way to handle this nonlinearity. They examine both its statistical properties and its computational properties, addressing the quality of the estimates as well as the work needed to obtain them. The estimator is therefore studied in the context of the compressed observations actually available.

A central question is how to allocate a fixed storage or transmission budget between more projections and greater bit depth per projection. This makes representation precision and representation size part of the same design problem. The paper also discusses the existence of a qualitative counterpart to the Johnson-Lindenstrauss lemma under quantization, connecting compressed similarity estimation with geometric preservation under dimensionality reduction.
neurips-2016-quantized-random-projection.tldr: The paper studies maximum likelihood estimation of cosine similarity from quantized projections under a fixed bit budget.

paragraphs: RETAIN addresses the need for health-record predictions that combine accuracy with understandable reasoning. The model uses two levels of neural attention to identify influential past visits and significant clinical variables within those visits. This gives the prediction an interpretation at both the encounter level and the level of information such as diagnoses.

The model processes attention in reverse chronological order, taking inspiration from how physicians review a patient's history. This arrangement makes recent visits likely to receive greater attention. The mechanism connects the temporal organization of the record with the model's assessment of which visits and variables are influential for its prediction.

The authors evaluate RETAIN on a health-system dataset containing 14 million visits from 263,000 patients over eight years. They report predictive accuracy and computational scalability comparable to state-of-the-art methods such as recurrent neural networks, with ease of interpretation comparable to traditional models. The findings support the possibility of combining strong predictive performance with accessible explanations of influential information in electronic health records.
neurips-2016-retain-an-interpretable-pre.tldr: RETAIN uses reverse-time, two-level attention to make health-record predictions interpretable while achieving accuracy comparable to recurrent networks.

paragraphs: The paper asks how recurrent neural networks can propagate uncertainty about a hidden state over time. It introduces stochastic recurrent neural networks by combining a deterministic recurrent network with a state-space model. The resulting generative model keeps nonlinear recurrent computation while also representing uncertainty along a sequence of latent states.

A key architectural choice is to separate deterministic and stochastic layers clearly. This allows a structured variational inference network to follow the factorization of the model's posterior distribution. In practical terms, the inference procedure is organized to reflect how uncertainty is structured in the generative model, while predictions can average over uncertain latent paths.

The authors report large improvements over prior state-of-the-art results on the Blizzard and TIMIT speech-modeling datasets. On polyphonic music modeling, performance is comparable to competing methods. The findings show strong benefits for the reported speech tasks while preserving a more qualified result for music, supporting the combination of recurrent nonlinear dynamics and explicit latent-state uncertainty as a useful sequential modeling approach.
neurips-2016-sequential-neural-models-wi.tldr: Combining recurrent networks with stochastic state-space layers improves reported speech-modeling results while remaining competitive on polyphonic music.

paragraphs: Some perception systems operate inside larger processes where a user or another component can evaluate candidate predictions. In those settings, producing several plausible hypotheses can be useful. The paper treats this as a learning problem for an ensemble of deep networks, with the goal of producing alternatives that work well when such an evaluator is available.

The authors introduce a stochastic-gradient approach that minimizes loss with respect to an oracle. This makes the usefulness of the ensemble's candidate set the training target. They describe the method as simple to implement, independent of the particular network architecture and loss function, and parameter-free.

Across the evaluated tasks and architectures, the approach achieves lower oracle error than existing methods. Qualitative examples also show that its different solutions often give interpretable representations of ambiguity in the task. These results concern the quality of alternatives available to an oracle, matching the intended setting where a downstream evaluator can assess the proposed solutions.
neurips-2016-stochastic-multiple-choice-.tldr: Stochastic multiple-choice learning trains deep ensembles to offer useful alternative predictions and reduces oracle error across evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: The paper extends stochastic variance-reduction methods such as SVRG and SAGA to convex-concave saddle-point problems with objectives split into many components. It presents large-scale algorithms with linear convergence for the class studied. The aim is to bring incremental optimization techniques to problems involving both minimization and maximization.

Although the algorithmic extension is straightforward, the analysis used for convex minimization does not transfer directly. The authors instead use monotone operators to establish convergence, also extending the algorithm's applicability to problems such as variational inequalities. They distinguish splitting an objective into functions from splitting it through partial derivatives and discuss the convex-concave requirement on the terms.

Nonuniform sampling is identified as important for efficiency in both the theoretical analysis and practical results. The methods can also be accelerated through an extension of the catalyst framework. The authors report that the resulting accelerated algorithm is superior to accelerated batch algorithms in their comparison. Together, these contributions combine a new convergence analysis with choices that improve incremental saddle-point optimization.
neurips-2016-stochastic-variance-reducti.tldr: Variance-reduced incremental algorithms extend to saddle-point problems, with monotone-operator convergence proofs and catalyst-based acceleration.

paragraphs: The paper addresses black-box optimization when several candidate points can be evaluated simultaneously. One example is testing multiple neural-network architectures using parallel computing resources. The decision is therefore which group of evaluations to run together, making batch selection part of how an optimization method uses the available computational resources.

The proposed parallel knowledge gradient method is a batch Bayesian optimization algorithm. By construction, it chooses a batch that is Bayes optimal for a one-step decision. That qualification matters: the stated optimality concerns the next batch under the Bayesian criterion. The authors also provide an efficient strategy for computing the batch prescribed by that criterion.

Experiments use both synthetic test functions and hyperparameter tuning for practical machine learning algorithms. The method finds global optima significantly faster than previous batch Bayesian optimization methods in those evaluations, with especially strong results when evaluations are noisy. The contribution combines a principled criterion for selecting simultaneous evaluations with a computational strategy and evidence of practical optimization gains.
neurips-2016-the-parallel-knowledge-grad.tldr: Parallel knowledge gradient selects one-step Bayes-optimal evaluation batches and empirically speeds optimization, particularly with noisy evaluations.

paragraphs: The paper studies estimating a function observed at locations on an equal-sided, multidimensional grid. It assumes the function's discrete total variation is bounded and derives the minimax squared-error rate in terms of the number of locations and that bound. This rate describes the best achievable worst-case accuracy over the specified function class.

Total variation denoising, also called the fused lasso, achieves this optimal rate. By contrast, the authors prove that every estimator formed as a linear transformation of the observations is suboptimal over the bounded-variation class. This includes Laplacian smoothing and Laplacian eigenmaps, showing a statistical cost to using these simpler methods for this class of denoising problems.

The conclusion changes for discrete Sobolev spaces, which impose a smaller function class in the sense considered by the paper. The authors derive minimax rates there and show that linear estimators, including those same Laplacian methods, can be optimal. They also investigate how total variation denoising adapts to these smaller spaces, making the assumed function class central to comparing methods.
neurips-2016-total-variation-classes-bey.tldr: Total variation denoising achieves optimal grid-estimation rates where linear smoothers fall short, although linear methods can be optimal on smaller Sobolev classes.

paragraphs: The paper investigates learning the three-dimensional structure underlying two-dimensional images. Its motivation is that a representation of scene structure can separate the underlying elements from the complexity of how they are rendered. The authors build deep generative models of 3D structures and use probabilistic inference to recover those structures from images.

A central result is that the generative models and their inference networks can be trained jointly, end to end, directly from 2D images. This training does not use ground-truth 3D labels. The model therefore learns both a representation of three-dimensional structure and a way to infer that structure through image-based training.

The authors demonstrate high-quality generated samples and report log-likelihoods on several datasets, including ShapeNet, establishing benchmarks for the approach. They present the work as a first demonstration that learning to infer 3D representations in a purely unsupervised manner is feasible. The significance is this demonstrated feasibility of recovering structured 3D representations without supplying labeled 3D targets during training.
neurips-2016-unsupervised-learning-of-3d.tldr: Deep generative models and inference networks can jointly learn to recover 3D structure from 2D images without ground-truth 3D labels.
